workers-comp-emr-premium.formula: manual = payroll/100 x class_rate; modified = manual x EMR; rate_per_100 = modified/payroll x 100; credit_or_debit = manual - modified.
workers-comp-emr-premium.edition: The workers-compensation manual premium and its experience modification (EMR / e-mod), by name.
workers-comp-emr-premium.freeAccess: The manual-premium and experience-mod computation is a standard published workers-comp rating method (NCCI-style); rates are user-supplied.
workers-comp-emr-premium.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
workers-comp-emr-premium.editionNote: Workers-compensation premium starts as manual premium = payroll per $100 x the class rate, then is multiplied by the experience modification rate (EMR, or e-mod) that compares the employer's loss history to peers: below 1.0 is a credit (good safety record), above 1.0 a debit. A lower EMR both cuts premium and, on many public and large-owner projects, is a bid-list qualifier (an EMR at or below 1.0 is a common threshold). Rates and the EMR shown are inputs; the rating bureau (NCCI or an independent state bureau) publishes the class rate and computes the official EMR. The bureau's rating governs.

assumptions.name: Manual premium
assumptions.value: manual = payroll/100 x class rate

assumptions.name: Experience mod
assumptions.value: modified = manual x EMR; below 1.0 credit, above 1.0 debit

assumptions.name: Bureau governs
assumptions.value: the rating bureau's published rate and official EMR govern

axle-load-distribution.formula: Lever-arm: moving the tandem d inches changes the trailer reaction by dW = trailer_load * d / L (L = kingpin-to-tandem). shift_per_hole = trailer * hole_spacing / L; holes = ceil(target_shift / shift_per_hole).
axle-load-distribution.edition: Per the federal axle/gross weight limits - 23 CFR 658.17 (20,000 lb single, 34,000 lb tandem, 80,000 lb gross; the common 12,000 lb steer figure is an axle rating, not a federal limit) and the federal Bridge Formula, by name; lever-arm statics is public.
axle-load-distribution.freeAccess: Free at ecfr.gov; cross-references the bridge-formula tile. FMCSA enforces.
axle-load-distribution.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
axle-load-distribution.editionNote: Single-method (lever-arm slide); sliding redistributes drive<->trailer only, cannot fix an over-gross load. Bridge-formula spacing may bind before the cap.

assumptions.name: Per-hole shift
assumptions.value: computed from the lever arm (trailer load * spacing / kingpin-to-tandem distance), not assumed

condensing-flue-condensate.formula: therms_per_hr = input_btu_hr / 100000; water_produced_lb_hr = therms_per_hr x water_lb_per_therm; condensate_gph = water_produced_lb_hr x condensing_fraction / 8.34. Natural gas produces ~9.4 lb water per therm.
condensing-flue-condensate.edition: Condensing appliance flue condensate rate from the water of combustion (methane stoichiometry) and the condensing fraction, by name; the appliance's rated condensate output, the local plumbing code (drain, trap, neutralizer), and the manufacturer's instructions govern.
condensing-flue-condensate.freeAccess: The water-of-combustion stoichiometry (CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O) is public physics; the fuel input, the water per therm, and the condensing fraction are the appliance's operating values.
condensing-flue-condensate.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
condensing-flue-condensate.editionNote: A high-efficiency condensing furnace, boiler, or water heater produces liquid condensate that has to be drained, and the flow rate sizes the drain line, the condensate pump, and any acid neutralizer. Burning natural gas creates water as a product of combustion: the reaction of methane, CH4 plus two O2 giving CO2 and two H2O, yields about 9.4 pounds of water for every therm, or 100,000 BTU, of gas burned. So an appliance firing at 100,000 BTU per hour makes roughly 9.4 pounds of water vapor an hour. A non-condensing appliance sends all of that vapor out the vent as a gas, but a condensing appliance deliberately cools the flue gas below its water dew point to recover the latent heat of vaporization, and in doing so it condenses a large fraction of the water -- typically around 0.8 to 0.9 at the low return-water temperatures that make condensing possible. The drained condensate is therefore the water produced multiplied by the condensing fraction, converted from pounds to gallons at 8.34 pounds per gallon: 9.4 times 0.85 divided by 8.34 is about 0.96 gallons per hour, so a 100,000 BTU per hour appliance drains roughly a gallon an hour, and a 150,000 BTU per hour boiler about a gallon and a half. Two practical points govern the drain design. First, the condensate is mildly acidic -- it absorbs carbon dioxide and trace combustion acids to a pH around 3 to 5 -- so plumbing codes increasingly require passing it through a limestone or marble-chip neutralizer before it enters cast-iron or copper waste piping or a septic system. Second, the drain must be trapped, pitched to flow, and protected from freezing. The 9.4 pounds per therm varies with the actual gas composition, and the condensing fraction rises as the return-water temperature falls. This is a sizing aid; the appliance's rated condensate output, the local plumbing code requirements for the drain, trap, and neutralizer, and the manufacturer's installation instructions govern.

assumptions.name: Water of combustion
assumptions.value: natural gas produces ~9.4 lb water per therm (CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O); condensate = water produced x condensing fraction / 8.34 lb/gal

assumptions.name: Condensing fraction + drain
assumptions.value: the condensed fraction rises as the return temperature falls: roughly 0.8-0.9 only at low return temperatures, much less at 120-140 F; full condensing is about 1.1 gph per 100,000 Btu (Hamilton Engineering); condensate is acidic (pH ~3-5) -- code may require a neutralizer, a trap, pitch, and freeze protection

flue-gas-dew-point.formula: lambda = 1 + excess_air_pct/100; water_fraction = 2 / (1 + 9.52 x lambda); p_h2o_mmhg = 760 x water_fraction; dew_point_c = 1730.63 / (8.07131 - log10(p_h2o_mmhg)) - 233.426 (Antoine, water); dew_point_f = dew_point_c x 9/5 + 32.
flue-gas-dew-point.edition: Natural-gas flue-gas water dew point from methane combustion stoichiometry and the Antoine water-saturation relation, by name; the appliance listing, the NFPA 54 (National Fuel Gas Code) / manufacturer vent-sizing tables, and the AHJ govern.
flue-gas-dew-point.freeAccess: The stoichiometry (CH4 + 2 O2 -> CO2 + 2 H2O) and the Antoine saturation equation are public physics; the excess-air level is the combustion setting.
flue-gas-dew-point.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
flue-gas-dew-point.editionNote: Natural gas is mostly methane, and burning it produces water: the balanced reaction CH4 + 2 O2 gives one molecule of carbon dioxide and two of water, so the combustion products carry a lot of water vapor, and the temperature at which that vapor begins to condense -- the flue-gas water dew point -- decides whether a vent, chimney, or heat exchanger stays dry or gets wet. Including the nitrogen that rides along with the combustion air and any excess air, the total moles of wet flue gas per mole of methane are one plus 9.52 times the air ratio lambda (lambda is 1 at stoichiometric, 1.15 at 15% excess air), while the water stays at two moles, so the water mole fraction is 2 divided by (1 plus 9.52 lambda). At stoichiometric that is about 19%; at 15% excess air it falls to 2 over (1 plus 9.52 times 1.15), or 16.7%, because the extra air dilutes the products. That fraction times atmospheric pressure gives the water vapor's partial pressure -- about 127 millimeters of mercury at 15% excess air -- and the Antoine saturation equation for water converts that partial pressure into the dew-point temperature, roughly 134 degrees Fahrenheit at 15% excess air, about 139 near stoichiometric, and lower as excess air increases. The practical consequence is central to venting: a standard, non-condensing appliance must keep its flue gas above about 135 degrees all the way to the vent terminal, because if a masonry chimney or a single-wall connector runs colder the flue gas condenses into a mildly acidic water that corrodes steel connectors and spalls chimney masonry -- the classic failure that a chimney liner or a Category I vent-sizing table exists to prevent. A condensing appliance does the opposite on purpose, dropping the flue gas below the dew point to recover the latent heat of that water and piping the resulting condensate to a drain. Note this is the WATER dew point; the sulfuric-acid dew point, which matters for oil and other higher-sulfur fuels, is considerably higher. The real value also shifts with the exact fuel composition, the humidity of the combustion air, and the altitude. This is a screening calculation; the appliance's listing and installation instructions, the NFPA 54 National Fuel Gas Code and the manufacturer's vent-sizing tables, and the authority having jurisdiction govern the venting.

assumptions.name: Methane combustion + Antoine
assumptions.value: water fraction = 2/(1 + 9.52*lambda); dew point from the Antoine water-saturation relation on the water partial pressure at 1 atm

assumptions.name: Venting consequence
assumptions.value: non-condensing appliances must stay above ~135 F to the terminus or the vent condenses acidic water (liner / Category I table); condensing appliances drop below on purpose

chlorine-decay-constant.formula: First-order decay C(t) = C0 x exp(-k x t) solved for the rate constant: k = ln(C0 / C) / t, from an initial residual C0 and a measured residual C over an elapsed time t (a distribution bottle test). Half-life = ln(2) / k.
chlorine-decay-constant.edition: EPA 815-R-02-020 (Effects of Water Age on Distribution System Water Quality); AWWA M14.
chlorine-decay-constant.governance: Estimate. Operator of record and primacy agency govern.
chlorine-decay-constant.editionNote: The back-calculated k is the field decay constant that feeds the forward chlorine-decay and booster-spacing model; it depends on temperature, TOC, and pipe material, so a bottle or pipe-loop test should reflect the actual water and conditions.

assumptions.name: Decay model
assumptions.value: bulk first-order C(t) = C0 e^(-kt)

assumptions.name: Measurement
assumptions.value: C is the residual measured after time t on the same water sample as C0

assumptions.name: Typical k
assumptions.value: 0.05-0.20 1/hr depending on TOC and temperature

lightning-countdown.formula: distance_mi = flash_to_bang_seconds / 5 (sound at sea level ~ 1125 ft/s). 30-30 rule: 30 s or less flash-to-bang (~6 mi or closer) -> seek shelter.
lightning-countdown.edition: NOAA / NWS lightning safety; 30-30 rule is a public guideline.
lightning-countdown.governance: Geometry is not forecasting. Avalanche advisory and incident commander govern.
lightning-countdown.editionNote: Single-edition (NOAA / NWS 30-30 rule; flash-to-bang distance is a physical fact, the speed of sound at sea level).

assumptions.name: Sound speed
assumptions.value: ~1125 ft/s at sea level; 5 s ~ 1 mi

assumptions.name: 30-30 rule threshold
assumptions.value: 30 s flash-to-bang (~6 mi); resume after 30 min of last detected strike

wet-bulb-psychrometer.formula: Sling psychrometer dry-bulb / wet-bulb pair → relative humidity, dew point, and grains per pound. Vapor pressure from the psychrometer relation e = e_s(Tw) - A x P x (Td - Tw) with A ≈ 0.000662 1/°C at sea level; saturation vapor pressure e_s by the August-Roche-Magnus approximation.
wet-bulb-psychrometer.edition: August-Roche-Magnus formulation by name; ASHRAE Fundamentals psychrometric chart by name.
wet-bulb-psychrometer.freeAccess: Psychrometric formulas free in published engineering texts.
wet-bulb-psychrometer.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.

assumptions.name: Atmospheric pressure
assumptions.value: 14.696 psi (sea level) unless user supplies

smoke-reading.formula: (reference page; no compute) Volume / velocity / density / color interpretation framework from Dave Dodson's 'Reading Smoke' methodology, by name.

smoke-reading.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed fire protection engineer govern.
smoke-reading.editionNote: Single-edition (NFA training-material framework; original plain-English summary).

sales-tax-compound.formula: Forward: tax = pre_tax * (rate1 + rate2). Reverse: pre_tax = post_tax / (1 + rate1 + rate2).
sales-tax-compound.edition: Arithmetic. No live rate lookup; user supplies state and local rates.
sales-tax-compound.freeAccess: Each state's department of revenue publishes its current rate; user is responsible for the rate.
sales-tax-compound.governance: Estimate. Verify before sending to your bookkeeper, banker, or CPA.
sales-tax-compound.editionNote: Single-edition (math). Per spec §3, this site does not aggregate live sales-tax rates.

assumptions.name: Compounding

assumptions.source: U.S. state tax convention; some jurisdictions tax differently - verify locally

ltv.formula: LTV = loan_amount / value. Conventional conforming loans require PMI when LTV > 80%. Value is the lesser of appraised value or purchase price (FNMA Selling Guide).
ltv.edition: FNMA Single-Family Selling Guide §B2-1.2-01 (current). FHA Handbook 4000.1 §II.A.2 (LTV caps; 96.5% maximum on purchase).
ltv.governance: Estimate. Lender governs final underwriting and rate / fee disclosure. Appraiser governs the appraised value. State law and the agency's program guidelines may impose stricter limits than the published thresholds.
ltv.editionNote: Underwriting thresholds change over time and by product (conventional / FHA / VA / specialty); the bands shown here are common-practice ranges. Lender governs final underwriting.

assumptions.value: user enters appraised value or purchase price; FNMA convention is the lesser

assumptions.source: FNMA / FHLMC convention; exact PMI rate is lender-set

piti.formula: Monthly P&I = (P * r) / (1 - (1 + r)^-n) where P is principal, r is APR/12, n is term in months. PITI = P&I + monthly_tax + monthly_insurance. Tax = annual_property_tax / 12; insurance = annual_premium / 12. HOA and PMI are user-supplied monthly line items; the total output (key piti_plus_hoa) includes both HOA and PMI.
piti.edition: Standard mortgage amortization. The closed-form annuity-payment formula is universal.
piti.freeAccess: Public reference; covered in any introductory finance text. CFPB Closing Disclosure form (public) shows the same line-item composition.
piti.governance: Estimate. Lender governs final underwriting and rate / fee disclosure. Appraiser governs the appraised value. State law and the agency's program guidelines may impose stricter limits than the published thresholds.
piti.editionNote: Single-edition (mathematical fact). The PMI rate lookup from LTV is a lender-specific table and is not bundled; the user enters the PMI line item.

closing-costs.freeAccess: Free at consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home. Forms H-24 / H-25 published in 12 CFR Part 1026 Appendix H.
closing-costs.governance: Estimate. Lender governs final underwriting and rate / fee disclosure. Appraiser governs the appraised value. State law and the agency's program guidelines may impose stricter limits than the published thresholds.
closing-costs.editionNote: Dollar ranges are common-case national midpoints; HCOL and LCOL markets vary materially. The lender's Loan Estimate (delivered within 3 business days of application) is the value of record. State and local transfer taxes vary by orders of magnitude (some states $0; others 1-2% of price).

assumptions.value: default mid-month closing assumption; actual closings may run 0 to 30 days

assumptions.value: RESPA permits up to 2 months as an initial deposit (12 CFR §1024.17(c)(1))

harmonic-resonance.formula: h_resonant = sqrt(MVA_sc / MVAR_cap); flag if h_resonant is within 0.5 of the 5th, 7th, 11th, or 13th harmonic.
harmonic-resonance.edition: Parallel-resonance order of a power-factor capacitor bank (IEEE 519 / IEEE 1531 harmonic filter and resonance guidance), first-principles, by name; a harmonic study governs.
harmonic-resonance.freeAccess: The h = sqrt(MVA_sc / MVAR_cap) resonance relation is a published first-principles result; the bus short-circuit level and the bank rating come from the system data.
harmonic-resonance.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
harmonic-resonance.editionNote: Parallel-resonance order of a power-factor capacitor bank. The PF capacitors and the system source inductance form a parallel LC circuit whose resonant order is h = sqrt(MVA_sc / MVAR_cap). If that order lands on a harmonic the nonlinear loads produce (the 5th, 7th, 11th, or 13th), the resonance amplifies it into damaging overvoltage and current that blow the capacitors or overheat transformers. A larger capacitor bank lowers the resonant order toward the strong low-order harmonics, so upsizing for power factor can create the problem. The estimate uses the bus short-circuit level and the bank rating and ignores load and resistive damping; a detuning reactor (making it a filter) or a harmonic study is the fix. A screening aid, not a harmonic study.

assumptions.name: Resonant order
assumptions.value: h = sqrt(MVA_sc / MVAR_cap) for the parallel cap-and-source-inductance circuit

assumptions.name: Bigger bank, lower order
assumptions.value: a larger capacitor bank lowers the resonant order toward the strong low harmonics

assumptions.name: Idealized
assumptions.value: ignores load and resistive damping; a detuning reactor or harmonic study is the fix

crane-net-capacity.formula: net = gross_chart - hook_block - jib - wire_rope; total_hook = load + below_hook; pct_of_net = total_hook / net x 100; flags at 75 / 90 / 100%.
crane-net-capacity.edition: ASME B30.5 (Mobile and Locomotive Cranes) and the manufacturer's load-chart notes by name for the deductions; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.1417(o) for the rule against exceeding rated capacity. Arithmetic on chart numbers.
crane-net-capacity.freeAccess: OSHA 1926 Subpart CC is free at osha.gov. The capacity numbers come from the manufacturer's load chart.
crane-net-capacity.governance: Estimate. Head rigger and manufacturer working-load-limit charts govern. Inspect every piece of hardware before the show.
crane-net-capacity.editionNote: The chart, the configuration (boom length, radius, outrigger spread, counterweight), and a qualified operator govern. Structural-vs-stability ratings and an out-of-level deration live on the chart. The 75 / 90 / 100% values are planning flags, not a substitute for the chart.

assumptions.name: Deduction stack
assumptions.value: hook block / overhaul ball, erected jib, and wire-rope deduction per the chart

assumptions.name: Flags
assumptions.value: 75% critical / engineered, 90% margin gone, 100% over chart (STOP)

reeving-parts-of-line.formula: frictionless_pull_lb = load_lb / parts_of_line; hauling_line_pull_lb = load_lb / (k + k^2 + ... + k^N) = load_lb x (1 - k) / (k (1 - k^N)) when the lead line leaves over a sheave (lead_sheave = 1, the default), or load_lb x (1 - k) / (1 - k^N) without one, with k = sheave_efficiency, N = parts_of_line (= load/N when k = 1, no lead sheave); reeving_efficiency = load_lb / (parts_of_line x hauling_line_pull_lb).
reeving-parts-of-line.edition: Block-and-tackle / hoist reeving efficiency (Wire Rope Users Manual / Crosby reeving practice; ASME B30 hoisting), by name; the block and rope ratings, the actual sheave friction, and a qualified rigger and the lift plan govern.
reeving-parts-of-line.freeAccess: The reeving-efficiency relation is public rigging mechanics; the per-sheave efficiency (~0.98 roller, 0.96 plain) is a standard published figure and the load and parts are the rig's values.
reeving-parts-of-line.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
reeving-parts-of-line.editionNote: When a load is lifted through a block and tackle -- a fixed block and a moving block reeved with several parts of line -- the mechanical advantage divides the load among the parts, but sheave friction makes the hauling line work harder than the ideal. In a frictionless system each of the N parts carries an equal share, load divided by N, and that share is what the hauling line must pull. Real sheaves each lose a few percent of the tension passing over them to bearing friction and the work of bending the rope, and crucially that loss stacks from part to part: the tension is highest in the part closest to the hauling end and falls by the per-sheave efficiency factor k across each successive sheave. Setting the sum of all the parts' tensions equal to the load and solving gives the load times (1 minus k) divided by (1 minus k raised to the N), and when the hauling line leaves the block over one more sheave, the usual case, that sheave costs another factor k, so the pull is the load divided by (k + k^2 + ... + k^N), the Crosby line-parts ratio. For a 20,000-pound load reeved on four parts with roller-bearing sheaves at k = 0.98, the pull over a lead sheave is 20,000 divided by (0.98 + 0.98^2 + 0.98^3 + 0.98^4), or about 5,258 pounds, noticeably above the frictionless 5,000 pounds; the reeving efficiency, defined as the load divided by N times the pull, is about 95.1%. Plain bronze-bushed sheaves run closer to k = 0.96 and cost more efficiency. Adding parts of line multiplies the load advantage but also stacks more friction, so doubling the number of parts never quite halves the required pull. Two cautions: this is the steady pull to hold or slowly haul the load, not the larger force needed to overcome inertia and start it moving, and it is the tension in the lead (hauling) line only. This is a rigging screen; the rated capacities of the blocks and rope, the true sheave friction for the specific hardware, the reeving pattern, and a qualified rigger working to the lift plan govern the actual rig.

assumptions.name: Reeving pull
assumptions.value: pull = load / (k + k^2 + ... + k^N) with a lead sheave, load x (1 - k) / (1 - k^N) without; frictionless share = load/N; efficiency = load/(N x pull)

assumptions.name: Per-sheave efficiency
assumptions.value: k ~0.98 roller-bearing, ~0.96 plain-bronze sheaves; loss stacks part to part; steady pull on the lead line only (not inertia to start)
assumptions.source: Wire Rope Users Manual / Crosby / ASME B30

welder-arc-circuit-conductor.formula: duty_multiplier from NEC Table 630.11(A): transformer / rectifier column = the printed rows (0.71 at 50%), sqrt(duty_pct / 100) between them, 0.45 at 20% or less; motor-generator column 1.00 / 0.96 / 0.91 / 0.86 / 0.81 / 0.75 / 0.69 / 0.62 at 100 to 30%, 0.55 at 20% or less, linear between rows; effective_current_a = primary_current_a x duty_multiplier; ocpd_max_a = 2.0 x primary_current_a (630.12(A)).
welder-arc-circuit-conductor.edition: NEC 630.11 (conductors) and 630.12 (overcurrent protection) for arc-welding equipment, with the Table 630.11(A) duty-cycle multipliers, by name; the welder nameplate and the adopted NEC edition govern.
welder-arc-circuit-conductor.freeAccess: The duty-cycle multipliers and the 200% OCPD limit are public NEC (many jurisdictions post the adopted NEC); the rated primary current and duty come from the welder nameplate.
welder-arc-circuit-conductor.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
welder-arc-circuit-conductor.editionNote: An arc-welder branch circuit is sized on an EFFECTIVE current rather than the nameplate primary. NEC 630.11(A) and Table 630.11(A) set the conductor at the rated primary current times a duty-cycle multiplier equal to the square root of the duty cycle, held at 0.45 for a duty of 20% or less where the table stops (a 50%-duty welder draws its rated current only half the time, so its I^2 t heating is halved and the conductor need only carry sqrt(0.5) = 0.71 of the primary). The conductor's ampacity must be at least this effective current. NEC 630.12(A) permits the overcurrent device to be up to 200% of the rated primary current (using the next standard size down if 200% does not land on one). This covers arc welders (transformer / rectifier / motor-generator); resistance (spot / seam) welders use the separate 630.31 / 630.32 method with a 300% OCPD limit. Use the welder's rated primary current and duty cycle; the AHJ, the welder nameplate, and the adopted NEC edition govern.

assumptions.name: Duty multiplier
assumptions.value: conductor at I_primary x the Table 630.11(A) multiplier for the welder type: transformer / rectifier (sqrt(duty) as printed, 0.45 at 20% or less) or motor-generator (the higher column, 0.55 at 20% or less); a low-duty welder heats the wire less

assumptions.name: OCPD 200%
assumptions.value: arc-welder overcurrent device up to 200% of the rated primary (630.12(A)); resistance welders use 630.31/32 (300%)

bearing-max-load.formula: p = 3 (ball) or 10/3 (roller); L10_rev = target_hr x 60 x rpm; P_max = C x (10^6 / L10_rev)^(1/p); the inverse of L10 = (C/P)^p x 10^6.
bearing-max-load.edition: The ISO 281 / ABMA 9 & 11 basic rating life (L10) solved for the maximum equivalent load, by name; the mounting, lubrication, and application govern.
bearing-max-load.freeAccess: The L10 rating-life relation is a published ISO 281 / ABMA result; the dynamic load rating C comes from the bearing catalog and the target life from the application.
bearing-max-load.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
bearing-max-load.editionNote: The largest equivalent dynamic load a bearing can carry and still reach a target L10 life, the inverse of bearing-l10-life: from L10 = (C/P)^p x 10^6 rev with L10 = target_hr x 60 x rpm, P_max = C x (10^6 / L10_rev)^(1/p), p = 3 ball / 10/3 roller. Because life scales as the cube (ball) of the load ratio, the load limit is only weakly sensitive to the target life (doubling the required hours cuts the allowable load by about 20% for ball), so a bearing sized for a long life still carries a fair load. The basic L10 assumes clean, well-lubricated operation; contamination, misalignment, and lubricant condition are handled by the modified aISO life. L10 is the life at which 10% has failed, not the average. A planning estimate, not a warranty; the mounting, lubrication, and application govern.

assumptions.name: Cube law inverse
assumptions.value: P_max scales as (10^6/L10_rev)^(1/p), p = 3 ball / 10/3 roller; the load limit is weakly sensitive to the target life

assumptions.name: Basic L10
assumptions.value: assumes clean, well-lubricated operation; contamination needs the modified aISO life

assumptions.name: 10% definition
assumptions.value: L10 is the life at which 10% have failed, not the average (L50 is ~5x)

curtain-wall-mullion-deflection.formula: line_load_pli = wind_pressure_psf x tributary_width_ft / 12; allowable_deflection_in = span/175 up to a 162 in span, otherwise span/240 + 0.25; required_i_in4 = 5 w L^4 / (384 E delta); moment_in_lb = w L^2 / 8.
curtain-wall-mullion-deflection.edition: Simple-span uniform-load deflection applied to a curtain wall mullion whose line load is the design wind pressure times the tributary width. The deflection limit is AAMA's for framing supporting glass -- L/175 up to a 13 ft 6 in span, L/240 plus a quarter inch beyond it -- cited by name and not reproduced. A screen, never a stamp; the glazing system manufacturer's published section properties, the project's wind design, and the engineer of record govern.
curtain-wall-mullion-deflection.freeAccess: The deflection relation is public mechanics of materials; the wind pressure, span, and tributary width come from the project, and the limit rule is cited to its standard rather than mirrored.
curtain-wall-mullion-deflection.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
curtain-wall-mullion-deflection.editionNote: A mullion is a simple beam spanning floor to floor, loaded by the wind pressure on the glass either side of it, so its line load is the pressure times the tributary width -- half a bay each way. Aluminium's elastic modulus is about a third of steel's, which is why aluminium framing is deflection-governed almost without exception: it has plenty of strength and not much stiffness, and the section that satisfies the deflection limit is invariably far larger than the section that satisfies the stress check. The deflection limit is not about occupant comfort. Glass is rigid and its sealant joints have limited movement capacity, so a frame that deflects too far either breaks the glass or opens the seal and leaks, and the limit switches from a pure ratio to a ratio-plus-constant on long spans because a pure ratio would eventually allow more movement than any sealant can accommodate. The span dominates everything: deflection goes as the span to the fourth power while the allowance goes only as the span, so the required stiffness scales as the cube. A thirty percent longer span needs more than twice the moment of inertia, and more still once the limit rule tightens, which is why curtain wall sections get visibly deeper as floor heights rise and why floor-to-floor height is the single most consequential input in a curtain wall's framing cost.

assumptions.name: Deflection limit
assumptions.value: AAMA L/175 for framing supporting glass up to a 13 ft 6 in span; L/240 + 1/4 in beyond it

assumptions.name: Simple span, uniform load
assumptions.value: floor-to-floor mullion pinned at both ends; a continuous or spliced mullion is a different model

assumptions.name: Stiffness scales as L cubed
assumptions.value: deflection goes as L^4 and the allowance as L, so span dominates the section size

static-rollover-threshold.formula: srt_g = (track_width_in / 2) / cg_height_in; rollover_speed_mph = sqrt(srt_g x 32.174 x curve_radius_ft) x 0.6818 (g = 32.174 ft/s^2, ft/s -> mph).
static-rollover-threshold.edition: Static stability factor (static rollover threshold), first-principles rigid-body statics; the track width and loaded CG height come from the truck and its load. NHTSA static-stability metric.
static-rollover-threshold.freeAccess: The static stability factor is a first-principles statics identity (half-track over CG height); the track width, loaded CG height, and curve radius are user-supplied.
static-rollover-threshold.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
static-rollover-threshold.editionNote: The static rollover threshold (static stability factor, SSF) is the steady lateral acceleration, in g, that lifts the inside wheels of a rigid vehicle: SRT = (track width / 2) / CG height. On a steady curve, rollover impends when the lateral acceleration v^2/R reaches SRT x g, giving a rollover speed sqrt(SRT x g x R). This is a STATIC, rigid-body screen: suspension roll, tire lateral slip, load shift, and the transient of a fast steer or a decreasing-radius ramp all lower the real threshold below the static value, so a driver must slow well below this on ramps and curves. A loaded van runs about 0.35 to 0.45 g, a low flatbed higher, a tanker or high-cube lower. The loaded CG height and the truck govern; the number is a screen, not a substitute for driving to conditions.

assumptions.name: Rigid body
assumptions.value: no suspension roll or tire slip; these lower the real threshold below the static value

assumptions.name: Steady curve
assumptions.value: the rollover speed assumes a constant-radius steady turn; a fast steer or ramp is worse

maglock-holding-leverage.formula: force at the handle = rated holding force x (lock distance from the hinge) / (handle distance from the hinge); an electromagnet's force follows the square of the supply voltage; the entered gap derate multiplies what is left.
maglock-holding-leverage.edition: The lever relation for a door hinged at one edge, by name, with the adopted codes named as governing electrically locked egress. Rated holding force is the manufacturer's figure and assumes full face contact at rated voltage.
maglock-holding-leverage.freeAccess: A lever ratio on dimensions the user measures, against a rated force from the manufacturer; no product table is reproduced.
maglock-holding-leverage.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
maglock-holding-leverage.editionNote: The door is a lever and the magnet is what it works against. A magnet mounted a few inches from the hinge on a three-foot door works at a large mechanical disadvantage against someone pulling at the handle, so a four-figure rating becomes a two-figure resistance, defeatable by one determined person. Mounting the same magnet near the strike edge changes the ratio to nearly one to one and the lock performs as rated, at no cost, which makes lock position the whole design. Two further reductions apply before anyone pulls. Rated holding force assumes full face contact between the armature and the magnet with no gap, and a warped door, paint, dirt, or a misaligned armature drops it sharply. And the magnet must have its rated voltage AT THE LOCK, which a long undersized run does not deliver; because force follows roughly the square of the supply voltage, a small shortfall costs more than it looks. A well-mounted magnet that is dirty and undervolted can end up back where a badly mounted one started. The egress caution is not optional: a magnet holds until it is de-energized, so on any door required for egress the release arrangement is a code matter, and a magnet that stays locked when the building is on fire is a fatality mechanism regardless of its rating.

assumptions.name: Lock position is the whole design
assumptions.value: near the hinge throws most of the rating away; near the strike edge keeps it

assumptions.name: Force follows the square of voltage
assumptions.value: so a small drop at the lock costs more holding force than it appears to

assumptions.name: Rated force assumes no gap
assumptions.value: a warped door, paint, dirt, or a misaligned armature drops it sharply

hdd-annular-pressure.formula: annular pressure = the mud column at 0.052 psi per foot per pound-per-gallon, plus the annular friction loss; the screening resistance = the soil's overburden pressure plus a cohesion term; the factor of safety is their ratio, evaluated at the SHALLOWEST station.
hdd-annular-pressure.edition: The mud-column and overburden relations by name, as a screen. The real limiting pressure comes from a cavity-expansion relation -- the Delft or Luger approach -- driven by the soil's strength and stiffness rather than its weight alone. The drilling contractor, the mud engineer, and the geotechnical engineer of record govern.
hdd-annular-pressure.freeAccess: Pressure arithmetic on the user's own soil and fluid figures; no proprietary model is reproduced.
hdd-annular-pressure.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
hdd-annular-pressure.editionNote: The mechanism is hydraulic fracture. The fluid in the annulus has a pressure; the soil above it has a strength and a weight. When the fluid pressure exceeds what the soil can resist, it opens a path and follows it, and the path usually goes up. Because the resisting pressure grows with depth, THE DANGER IS USUALLY AT THE SHALLOW PARTS OF A BORE -- the entry, the exit, and any high point -- not at the deepest point under the crossing, which is where people instinctively worry and where the margin is usually largest. With a cohesive soil and a light, low-friction annulus the deep station can govern, so both stations are checked. Annular pressure is not just the mud column. Friction along the annulus adds to it, and that friction rises with pump rate, with a viscous fluid, and with a hole that is not clean and is loading up with cuttings, so a bore that was fine on the pilot can frac out during reaming when the annulus is smaller relative to the flow and the cuttings load is higher. The practical controls follow directly: keep the pump rate no higher than hole cleaning requires, keep the fluid properties right, ream in stages rather than one large pass, and maintain the deepest practical profile through the sensitive zone. Monitoring for returns at the surface during the bore is the last line, not the plan.

assumptions.name: The shallow station usually governs
assumptions.value: resistance grows with depth, so the margin is usually thinnest at entry, exit, and any high point; both stations are checked

assumptions.name: Friction is the term that changes when reaming
assumptions.value: a smaller annulus and a heavier cuttings load raise it above the pilot

assumptions.name: This is a screen, not a Delft analysis
assumptions.value: the real limiting pressure comes from cavity expansion in the soil's strength and stiffness

wood-screw-withdrawal.formula: W = 2,850 G^2 D (lb/in); Z_w = W x p_thread x CD.
wood-screw-withdrawal.edition: The NDS 2018 12.2.2 reference wood-screw withdrawal design value, by name; the 2,850 empirical constant is named.
wood-screw-withdrawal.freeAccess: The NDS is free to view at awc.org (ANSI/AWC NDS); the 12.2.2 wood-screw-withdrawal equation is in the published standard.
wood-screw-withdrawal.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
wood-screw-withdrawal.editionNote: The NDS 2018 12.2.2 reference withdrawal W = 2,850 G^2 D (lb/in) with G the holding member's specific gravity and D the screw diameter, the capacity W x thread penetration, and the load-duration CD. This returns the axial (withdrawal) wood-screw design value - withdrawal scales with the square of the specific gravity, so a screw that holds in Douglas Fir-Larch (G 0.50) can strip in a softer spruce (G 0.42) - and it does not cover the lateral connection or the head pull-through. A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record's stamped design.

assumptions.name: Withdrawal value
assumptions.value: W = 2,850 G^2 D per inch of penetration

assumptions.name: G^2 sensitivity
assumptions.value: the square-of-specific-gravity law makes species the dominant variable

assumptions.name: Axial only
assumptions.value: the withdrawal value, not the lateral connection or the head pull-through

wood-tension-bending.formula: ft = T/A; fb = M/S; Eq. 3.9-1 ft/Ft' + fb/Fb* <= 1.0 (Fb* = Fb' excluding CL); Eq. 3.9-2 (fb - ft)/Fb** <= 1.0 (Fb** = Fb' excluding CV).
wood-tension-bending.edition: The NDS 2018 3.9.1 bending-and-axial-tension interaction, Eq. 3.9-1 and 3.9-2, by name.
wood-tension-bending.freeAccess: The NDS is free to view at awc.org (ANSI/AWC NDS); the worked check is a free Missouri S&T course solution (CE 5260, Problem 7-5).
wood-tension-bending.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
wood-tension-bending.editionNote: Checked against the Missouri S&T CE 5260 Problem 7-5 solution: a 2x6 No. 1 DF-L truss bottom chord (A 8.25 sq in, S 7.563 cu in), D+S case, T 5,640 lb, M 3,000 in-lb, Ft' 1,009 psi, Fb' 1,495 psi (CD 1.15, CF 1.3, CL 1.0): 684/1,009 + 397/1,495 = 0.943 and (397 - 684)/1,495 = -0.192. This computes 0.9429 and -0.1920.

assumptions.name: Fb*
assumptions.value: Fb' with every applicable factor except the beam stability factor CL

assumptions.name: Fb**
assumptions.value: Fb' with every applicable factor except the volume factor CV; blank uses Fb*

assumptions.name: Area
assumptions.value: the user enters the net area where fastener holes reduce the section

trap-speed-horsepower.edition: Hale's empirical quarter-mile relations HP = weight x (mph/234)^3 and ET = 5.825 x (weight/HP)^(1/3), as compiled in the drag-racing references, by name.
trap-speed-horsepower.freeAccess: Hale's quarter-mile relations are public empirical results widely used in the drag-racing community.
trap-speed-horsepower.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
trap-speed-horsepower.editionNote: Hale's empirical quarter-mile relations HP = weight x (mph/234)^3 and ET = 5.825 x (weight/HP)^(1/3), with weight the race weight including driver (lb) and mph the trap speed. This returns an empirical horsepower estimate from the timeslip - it is a statistical fit to typical cars (the 234 constant and the cube law average out aerodynamics, driveline loss, and traction; a very slippery or very draggy car deviates), estimates flywheel (crank) power, and is not a substitute for a dyno. A hobbyist estimate; the actual dyno measurement governs.

assumptions.name: Trap-speed power
assumptions.value: HP = weight x (mph/234)^3, a cube-law fit to the power-to-weight ratio

assumptions.name: ET companion
assumptions.value: ET = 5.825 x (weight/HP)^(1/3) cross-checks the estimate

assumptions.name: Empirical
assumptions.value: a statistical fit estimating flywheel (crank) power; not a dyno measurement

product-pull-down-time.formula: hours = Q / capacity_btuh, with Q from the product pull-down relation (above freezing Q = m cp (t_enter - t_storage); freezing Q = m cp_above (t_enter - t_freeze) + m hif + m cp_below (t_freeze - t_storage); product entering at or below its freezing point: Q = m cp_below (t_enter - t_storage), no latent term). The inverse of product-pull-down-load (which returns rate = Q / hours).
product-pull-down-time.edition: The product pull-down time from the sensible-plus-latent cooling load and the available capacity, from ASHRAE Refrigeration, by name.
product-pull-down-time.freeAccess: The sensible-plus-latent product-cooling load is standard published refrigeration practice; the property tables are in the ASHRAE Handbook - Refrigeration.
product-pull-down-time.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
product-pull-down-time.editionNote: The pull-down time = the total product heat / the refrigeration capacity dedicated to the product load. Q is the same sensible (and, for a freezer, latent-plus-frozen-sensible) heat as product-pull-down-load. When the returned time exceeds the design window (commonly 24 h), add capacity or stage the loading. A sizing aid; the ASHRAE Refrigeration product-property tables govern.

assumptions.name: Time
assumptions.value: hours = Q / capacity, the inverse of rate = Q / hours

assumptions.name: Heat Q
assumptions.value: same sensible + latent product load as product-pull-down-load

assumptions.name: Property tables
assumptions.value: specific heats, freezing points, and latent heats from ASHRAE

rc-min-shear-reinforcement.formula: Av,min/s = max(0.75 sqrt(f'c) bw/fyt, 50 bw/fyt); s(Av,min) = Av / (Av,min/s); trigger = phi lambda sqrt(f'c) bw d; Vs,max = 8 sqrt(f'c) bw d; phi Vn,max = phi (2 lambda sqrt(f'c) bw d + Vs,max); s <= min(d/2, 24 in), or min(d/4, 12 in) when Vs > 4 sqrt(f'c) bw d. (phi = 0.75)
rc-min-shear-reinforcement.edition: The ACI 318-19 9.6.3.4 minimum shear reinforcement, the 9.6.3.1 Av,min trigger, the 22.5.1.2 Vs section-size ceiling, and the 9.7.6.2.2 stirrup-spacing maxima, by name.
rc-min-shear-reinforcement.freeAccess: ACI 318 is readable free through the ACI online reading room at concrete.org; 9.6.3, 9.7.6.2.2, and 22.5.1.2 are in the published code.
rc-min-shear-reinforcement.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
rc-min-shear-reinforcement.editionNote: The ACI 318-19 detailing and section-size checks that accompany a beam-shear strength calculation: 9.6.3.4 Av,min/s as the greater of 0.75 sqrt(f'c) bw/fyt and 50 bw/fyt (the 50 bw/fyt floor governs below about f'c = 4,444 psi); 9.6.3.1, which requires Av,min wherever Vu exceeds phi lambda sqrt(f'c) bw d -- the 2019 edition replaced the 318-14 'Vu > 0.5 phi Vc' trigger with this expression; 22.5.1.2, which caps the stirrup contribution at Vs = 8 sqrt(f'c) bw d so the section has an absolute ceiling of phi (Vc + 8 sqrt(f'c) bw d) regardless of reinforcement; and 9.7.6.2.2, which caps spacing at the lesser of d/2 and 24 in, halved to d/4 and 12 in once Vs exceeds 4 sqrt(f'c) bw d. Vc uses the simplified Table 22.5.5.1(a) expression appropriate to a member carrying at least Av,min. The Table 9.6.3.1 exemptions (shallow beams with h <= 10 in, one-way joist systems, certain slab-integral members) are NOT modeled, nor are torsion, deep-beam action, or prestressed members. A design aid, not a substitute for the structural engineer of record's stamped design.

assumptions.name: Minimum area
assumptions.value: Av,min/s is the greater of 0.75 sqrt(f'c) bw/fyt and 50 bw/fyt; the constant floor governs at ordinary strengths

assumptions.name: 2019 trigger
assumptions.value: Av,min required where Vu > phi lambda sqrt(f'c) bw d, replacing the 318-14 0.5 phi Vc rule; Table 9.6.3.1 exemptions not modeled

assumptions.name: Section ceiling
assumptions.value: Vs may not exceed 8 sqrt(f'c) bw d, so beyond phi (Vc + Vs,max) the section must grow

assumptions.name: Spacing maxima
assumptions.value: lesser of d/2 and 24 in, halved to d/4 and 12 in once Vs exceeds 4 sqrt(f'c) bw d

sprinkler-pressure-demand.formula: P1 = (q_head_gpm / k_factor)^2; pf = 4.52 x q_total_gpm^1.85 / (c_factor^1.85 x pipe_id_in^4.87); friction = pf x equiv_length_ft; elevation = 0.433 x elevation_ft; demand = P1 + friction + elevation.
sprinkler-pressure-demand.edition: NFPA 13 (Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems), 2022, by name; the Hazen-Williams friction coefficient 4.52 and exponents 1.85 / 4.87, the pipe-type C values, the 0.433 psi/ft water column, and the K-factor discharge relation Q = K sqrt(P) are the NFPA 13 hydraulic-calculation method.
sprinkler-pressure-demand.freeAccess: NFPA 13 is viewable free of charge through NFPA's online free-access reader; the Hazen-Williams friction, K-factor, and elevation arithmetic is public.
sprinkler-pressure-demand.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
sprinkler-pressure-demand.editionNote: NFPA 13 (Standard for the Installation of Sprinkler Systems), 2022 hydraulic method: the pressure demand at the base of the riser is the start pressure at the hydraulically most remote sprinkler P1 = (Q_head / K)^2 (the K-factor discharge relation Q = K sqrt(P)), plus the Hazen-Williams friction loss p = 4.52 Q^1.85 / (C^1.85 d^4.87) psi per foot carried over the governing run's equivalent length, plus the elevation head 0.433 psi per foot to lift the water to the head. The Hazen-Williams C defaults are the NFPA 13 pipe-type values (black or galvanized steel 120 in wet systems but 100 in dry and preaction systems, 150 copper or listed CPVC, 100 unlined cast iron), the equivalent length is the actual pipe plus the fitting/valve equivalents from the NFPA 13 fitting table, and the 7 psi minimum operating pressure at the end sprinkler is the standard-spray floor (flagged, not enforced). This assembles one representative flowing path; a full stamped design balances every node, branch, and grid loop in the remote area. A design aid, not a stamped hydraulic submittal - a qualified fire-protection engineer and the AHJ govern.

assumptions.name: Hazen-Williams C
assumptions.value: the pipe-roughness default is the NFPA 13 pipe-type value (black or galvanized steel 120 wet, 100 dry or preaction; 150 copper or listed CPVC; 100 unlined cast iron), editable; the diameter is the actual internal diameter, not the nominal size

assumptions.name: Equivalent length
assumptions.value: the entered length is the actual pipe run plus the fitting and valve equivalent lengths from the NFPA 13 fitting table; the tile does not tabulate fittings itself

assumptions.name: Single representative path
assumptions.value: the demand is assembled over one flowing path at a single total flow; a full stamped design balances every node, branch, and grid loop in the remote area, and the 7 psi end-sprinkler minimum is flagged, not enforced

flood-cut-takeoff.formula: cut_line_lf = perimeter_ft; drywall_sf = perimeter_ft x (cut_height_in/12) x faces; sheets = ceil(drywall_sf / 32); insulation_sf = perimeter_ft x (cut_height_in/12) when present; baseboard_lf = perimeter_ft when present.
flood-cut-takeoff.edition: ANSI/IICRC S500 flood-cut demolition practice by name; the geometry and the 32 ft^2 standard 4x8 sheet are not edition-bound.
flood-cut-takeoff.freeAccess: The flood-cut takeoff is pure wall geometry; the standard 4x8 board is 32 ft^2. The moisture meter governs the cut line.
flood-cut-takeoff.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
flood-cut-takeoff.editionNote: Single-edition (the wall geometry and the 32 ft^2 sheet do not roll). Cut a few inches above the highest moisture-meter reading - the meter governs the line, not a round number; the 12 / 24 / 48 in heights are common screens. ANSI/IICRC S500 names the flood-cut practice.

assumptions.name: Cut line
assumptions.value: the cut height is a screen; cut a few inches above the highest moisture-meter reading, not at a round number

assumptions.name: Sheet area
assumptions.value: standard 4x8 drywall = 32 ft^2 per sheet

assumptions.name: Scope
assumptions.value: linear and area takeoff only; the moisture map and the inspector govern how much wall comes out

cavity-drying-system.formula: bays = ceil(affected_wall_ft x 12 / stud_spacing_in); ports = bays x ports_per_bay; systems = ceil(ports / ports_per_system).
cavity-drying-system.edition: Bays-from-length geometry, by name; ANSI/IICRC S500. The stud-bay and system counts are field-arithmetic identities, not edition-bound.
cavity-drying-system.freeAccess: Sizes the injection / wall-cavity drying method - the minimally invasive alternative to a flood cut for drying enclosed assemblies in place.
cavity-drying-system.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
cavity-drying-system.editionNote: Single-edition (the bay geometry does not roll). Port count, airflow per port, and ports per system are equipment-MANUFACTURER specific (the bundled defaults are typical, not prescriptive). Cavity air-pressure direction must respect contamination - do NOT push Category 2/3 cavity air into clean spaces. The cavity-drying decision versus a flood cut and access drilling follow ANSI/IICRC S500, which GOVERNS.

assumptions.name: Manufacturer defaults
assumptions.value: ports per bay (default 1) and ports per system (default 12) are typical, not prescriptive

assumptions.name: Contamination direction
assumptions.value: do not push Category 2/3 cavity air into clean spaces

branch-saddle-cutback.formula: r = branch_od_in / 2; R = run_od_in / 2; cutback(theta) = R - sqrt(R^2 - (r sin theta)^2), theta around the branch from the run-axis line; max_cutback = R - sqrt(R^2 - r^2) at theta = 90; zero at theta = 0 (heel/toe).
branch-saddle-cutback.edition: The cylinder-intersection contour geometry, by name; the Pipe Fabrication Institute branch-layout practice. Not edition-bound.
branch-saddle-cutback.freeAccess: The saddle contour is the intersection of two cylinders, a closed-form square-root expression in the two radii; the geometry is public.
branch-saddle-cutback.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
branch-saddle-cutback.editionNote: Single-edition (the geometry does not roll). This is the geometric contour for a 90-DEGREE, SAME-CENTERLINE branch; the weld bevel, gap, and root face are added per the WPS, and a reducing or angled branch shifts the contour. A fit-up aid, not a weld procedure. PFI names the layout practice.

assumptions.name: Geometry
assumptions.value: a 90-degree, same-centerline branch on the run; branch OD <= run OD

assumptions.name: Weld prep
assumptions.value: the bevel, gap, and root face are added to the geometric contour per the WPS

assumptions.name: Stations
assumptions.value: marks per quarter (default 6 = every 15 degrees) set the ordinate spacing

masonry-cleaning-dilution.formula: diluted solution = area / coverage; one part concentrate to N parts water is one part in N+1, so concentrate = diluted / (N+1) and water is the remainder; prewet and rinse water are counted at their own rates per 100 sq ft.
masonry-cleaning-dilution.edition: The dilution and coverage identities by name. NO CLEANER, DILUTION OR COVERAGE IS SHIPPED: all three come from the manufacturer for the specific unit, and a test panel is required rather than advisable. The prefilled dilution and coverage are the worked example's, not a recommendation. Acid attacks polished stone, limestone, marble, many coloured and glazed units, and metal the runoff reaches. The cleaner manufacturer's instructions, the project specification, a test panel, and the applicable environmental rules govern.
masonry-cleaning-dilution.freeAccess: Two divisions on a dilution and a coverage rate the reader has; no product data is reproduced.
masonry-cleaning-dilution.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
masonry-cleaning-dilution.editionNote: THE CONCENTRATION IS A PROPERTY OF THE MASONRY RATHER THAN OF THE SOILING. Acid cleaners attack the cement paste in the mortar and the surface of many units, so the correct dilution is the weakest that removes the soiling, established on a test panel -- and strengthening it because the wall is dirty is the standard way to burn a facade, with damage that appears after the scaffold is down and is permanent. Prewetting keeps the cleaner on the surface rather than letting dry masonry draw it in, where it attacks the mortar from within and leaves salts that migrate out for years. Rinsing is a quantity as well as an action: residual cleaner keeps working, and an inadequate rinse produces damage that shows up days later on a wall that looked finished.

assumptions.name: Dilution and coverage are the manufacturer's
assumptions.value: for the specific unit, and a test panel is required

assumptions.name: Some units must never see acid
assumptions.value: polished stone, limestone, marble, coloured and glazed units, and metal below

assumptions.name: Containment and disposal are regulated
assumptions.value: and are not addressed here

feeder-loss-load-factor.formula: peak loss = 3 x peak current squared x total resistance; loss factor = k x load factor + (1 - k) x load factor squared, k entered (0.3 common; RUS 1724D-107 and 1724E-301 use 0.2); annual loss energy = peak loss x loss factor x 8,760 hours; energy delivered = peak demand x load factor x 8,760 hours.
feeder-loss-load-factor.edition: The three-phase I2R loss relation and the standard distribution loss-factor approximation, by name. The 0.3 and 0.7 coefficients are a widely used approximation rather than a measurement, and utilities carry their own. Load treated as concentrated at the far end, so the answer is an upper bound. The utility's loss study and its metered load data govern.
feeder-loss-load-factor.freeAccess: A square, a blend of two terms, and a multiplication by the hours in a year; no utility loss study is reproduced.
feeder-loss-load-factor.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed professional govern.
feeder-loss-load-factor.editionNote: Loss is quadratic in a current that varies all day, so the average of the square is not the square of the average, and the ratio between them is the loss factor. It is bounded by the square of the load factor at one end and the load factor itself at the other -- a perfectly flat load loses at the load factor, a load that is either at peak or off loses at its square -- and the 0.3 / 0.7 blend is the long-standing utility approximation between them. Taking peak loss for all 8,760 hours reads several times too high; using the load factor alone is still tens of percent high. The consequence runs the way people do not expect: a poor load factor means the savings from reconductoring or capacitor placement are SMALLER than a peak-based estimate promises.

assumptions.name: Load concentrated at the far end
assumptions.value: a uniformly distributed load loses about a third as much

assumptions.name: Conductor loss only
assumptions.value: transformer core and copper losses are usually the larger share

assumptions.name: The 0.3 / 0.7 coefficients are an approximation
assumptions.value: utilities carry their own from metered data

building-outage-cooldown.formula: tau = C / UA (h); T_eq = T_out + Q_internal / UA with about 250 Btu/h per person; T(t) = T_eq + (T_start - T_eq) x e^(-t / tau); hours to a threshold = tau x ln((T_start - T_eq) / (T_threshold - T_eq)), never reached when the threshold is at or below T_eq.
building-outage-cooldown.edition: The lumped-capacitance (Newton cooling) model by name, with the hours-of-safety thermal-resilience metric of Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Assessing thermal resilience of an assisted living facility during heat waves and cold snaps with power outages (OSTI 1984644), and material specific heats per ASHRAE Handbook -- Fundamentals by chapter. The UA comes from building-ua; the capacitance is entered or built from masses.
building-outage-cooldown.freeAccess: The LBNL report is free at osti.gov (OSTI 1984644); the method is a textbook first-order decay on the user's own UA and capacitance, and no ASHRAE table is reproduced -- four round specific heats are physical data.
building-outage-cooldown.governance: Estimate. AHJ and licensed mechanical contractor govern. ACCA Manual J / D / S supersede rules of thumb.
building-outage-cooldown.editionNote: A building without heat cools fast at first and slower as it nears the temperature it settles toward, and the pace is one number, the time constant: stored heat per degree over lost heat per degree. A heavy, tight building coasts for days and a light, leaky one for hours, so an envelope upgrade that lowers UA is also a resilience upgrade. People matter at the margin: at about 250 Btu/h each, a family of four in a small house raises the settling point by several degrees, and gathering in one room concentrates that heat. The single-node model errs in a known direction: the room air and light surfaces fall faster than the curve in the first hours, and pipes in exterior walls and crawl spaces freeze well before the room does. The capacitance dominates the answer and is an estimate; a measured cooldown from a previous outage is the best calibration. Carbon monoxide from improvised indoor heating kills people in every winter outage and is outside this tile.
